posts.title: Why fast websites quietly win every time
posts.excerpt: Speed is not a technical detail. It decides who stays, who buys and who comes back.

content.text: Nobody ever leaves a website and says, 'That was wonderfully slow.' Yet speed is usually the last thing discussed in a project kickoff, long after colours, fonts and animations have been argued over.
That is a mistake. A fast site feels trustworthy before a visitor reads a single word. A slow one feels broken, even when everything on it works.
Speed is a design decision
Every image, font and script you add has a cost. The fastest sites are not the ones with clever tricks at the end, they are the ones where someone said no early and often.
A page that loads in one second and a page that loads in three are not the same product.
Where the time actually goes

items: Oversized images served at full resolution to every device
Fonts that block text from appearing
Third-party scripts nobody remembers adding
Client-side rendering for content that never changes

content.caption: Most of the weight on a typical page is images.

content.text: A simple starting checklist
Compress and resize images, preload only the font weights you use, defer anything non-essential and render static content on the server. None of this is glamorous. All of it works.
Fast websites win quietly. Visitors do not notice the speed, they just stay a little longer, click a little more and come back a little sooner.

posts.title: Designing for the smallest screen first
posts.excerpt: Starting on a phone forces better decisions. Here is how we plan layouts from the inside out.

content.text: Most of your visitors are holding a phone. It is strange, then, how many designs begin on a wide desktop canvas and get squeezed down at the end.
We flip the order. The smallest screen comes first, because it has the least room for anything that does not matter.
Constraints make better layouts
On a 375 pixel screen you cannot hide behind whitespace or decoration. You have to decide what the page is about, what comes first and what the visitor should do next.
Start with the content order
Write the page as a single column. If the story still makes sense top to bottom, the wide version will be easy.
If it works in one column, it will work in three.
Then grow outward

items: Add columns only when content genuinely sits side by side
Make tap targets at least 44 pixels
Keep line lengths comfortable on every width
Test with a thumb, not a cursor

content.text: Designing small first is not about limiting the large screen. It is about making sure nothing on it is accidental.

posts.title: Plan the SEO before you plan the design
posts.excerpt: Page structure, keywords and internal links shape a site more than most people expect.

content.text: SEO is often treated as a coat of paint applied after launch. By then the structure is fixed, the URLs are set and the pages are built around the wrong questions.
Start with what people search for
Before a wireframe exists, list the questions your customers ask. Each strong question deserves a page of its own, and that list becomes your site map.

content.caption: A site map drawn from real search questions.

content.text: Structure carries meaning

items: One clear h1 per page that matches the search intent
Headings that outline the page like a table of contents
Short, readable URLs
Internal links that connect related pages

content.text: Design decides how a page looks. Structure decides whether anyone finds it.
Do it in the right order
Research, structure, content, then design. When the design arrives last, it has something real to serve instead of something imaginary to decorate.

posts.title: Motion that actually means something
posts.excerpt: Animation should guide attention, not compete for it. A few rules we follow with GSAP.

content.text: Animation is easy to overdo. When everything moves, nothing stands out, and the page starts to feel like it is performing instead of helping.
Three rules we follow

items: Move things to show what changed, not to fill silence
Keep one hero moment per page and let the rest stay calm
Always respect reduced motion preferences

content.text: A small example
A heading that slides up once on load is enough. Here is the pattern we reuse most often:
Good motion answers a question the visitor was about to ask.
If an animation does not guide, confirm or reveal something, cut it. Your page will feel faster and your best moments will land harder.

posts.title: Lessons from shipping Next.js to production
posts.excerpt: Caching, rendering modes and the small mistakes that cost us the most time.

content.text: Next.js makes it easy to build something that works on your laptop. Production is where the details start to matter.
Pick the rendering mode on purpose
Static, server-rendered and client-rendered pages all have a place. Our mistake early on was using the same mode everywhere because it was the default.

items: Static for pages that rarely change, such as blog posts
Server rendering for pages that depend on the visitor
Client rendering only for truly interactive pieces

content.text: Caching is where the surprises live
Stale data is rarely a bug in your code. It is usually a cache you forgot you configured. Write down what is cached, for how long and what clears it.
export const revalidate = 3600; // refresh at most once an hour
Small mistakes, big costs
Unoptimised images, giant client bundles and missing error pages cost us more hours than any hard problem. Boring checklists are underrated.
Most production bugs are decisions we never made on purpose.

posts.title: How a Bugsmoker project actually runs
posts.excerpt: From first call to launch day: the rhythm we use to keep small projects calm and fast.

content.text: Small projects go wrong in boring ways: unclear goals, late feedback, surprise scope. Our process exists to prevent those, not to look impressive.
Four steps, every time

items: Discover: goals, audience and what success looks like
Design: structure and visuals reviewed with you
Build: clean, tested code with early progress to see
Support: hosting and improvements after launch

content.text: Why the rhythm matters
You hear from us weekly, you see real progress early and there are no big reveals at the end. Surprises are fun at birthdays, not at launches.
Calm projects are fast projects.
After launch we stay close. Monitoring, fixes and small improvements are part of the work, not an upsell.

posts.title: Core Web Vitals in plain words
posts.excerpt: What the three metrics measure, why they matter and the quickest ways to improve them.

content.text: Core Web Vitals sound technical, but each one answers a simple human question about your page.
The three metrics
LCP: how fast does it appear?
Largest Contentful Paint measures how long the main content takes to show up. Aim for under two and a half seconds.
INP: how quickly does it respond?
Interaction to Next Paint tracks how soon the page reacts after a tap or click. Heavy scripts are the usual culprit.
CLS: does it jump around?
Cumulative Layout Shift measures unexpected movement. Reserve space for images and ads so nothing pushes the text away.
Quick wins

items: Set width and height on every image
Preload the hero image
Split large scripts and load them later
Use system fonts or font-display: swap

content.text: Fix the biggest image first. It is almost always the answer.

posts.title: Why your app should work without a signal
posts.excerpt: Offline-first thinking makes apps feel faster and more trustworthy, even on good connections.

content.text: Connections drop in lifts, trains and basements. An app that goes blank at that moment teaches people not to rely on it.
Local first, network second
In an offline-first app, the screen reads from local storage and the network syncs in the background. Taps feel instant because they do not wait for a server.

content.caption: The app keeps working when the signal does not.

content.text: What it takes

items: A local database as the source of truth
A queue of changes waiting to sync
Clear rules for resolving conflicts
A calm indicator that shows sync status

content.text: Trust is built in the moments when the network fails.
It is more work up front, but the payoff is an app that feels fast everywhere, including places where connectivity is great.

posts.title: Small studio, big opinions
posts.excerpt: What we believe about craft, speed and keeping things fun while doing serious work.

content.text: We are a small team, and we like it that way. Fewer people means fewer handoffs, and fewer handoffs means fewer things lost in translation.
What we believe

items: Craft beats volume
Fast beats flashy
Honest timelines beat optimistic ones
Work can be serious without being stiff

content.text: Take the work seriously. Take yourself lightly.
If that sounds like the kind of team you want in your corner, say hello. We would love to hear what you are building.
